title: Tackan
summary: Tackan is recorded as a tract of land in Smithtown on the Nissequogue River.
ancestral_territory_note: Shown in relation to Setauket Ancestral Land on the current ancestral territory map.
why_this_matters: In 1704, English speculators surveyed and purchased a massive 24,283-acre tract of Indigenous territory along the Nissequogue River under the Native name Tackan. Examining the sheer scale of these early colonial land acquisitions reveals how rapidly Native communities were systematically dispossessed of their vast, resource-rich ancestral territories to fuel European expansion.
history_content: The name appears in 1704 land records involving Benjamin Aske and Company. Because the tract was extensive, it can be associated only broadly with the Nissequogue River and Smithtown area.
translation_content:
Tackan is interpreted as woodland, forest, or wild lands, comparing it with Delaware-language forms for woods.

Why Place Names Matter

“Names like these convey detailed and exact geographical information, encoding knowledge of the land within the name itself.”

— Aliana Violet Parker, Learning the Language of the Land: A Review and Analysis of U.S. Federal Policy on Native American Sacred Places (2012), Printed p. 30
preservation_content: Tackan preserves a land-record name for a large wooded tract along the Nissequogue River, where colonial surveys and purchase licenses transformed Native homelands into mapped property.
